question: When seated for proper body position, your arms should be:
choice_a: Slightly bent when holding the handgrips
choice_d: Held as far apart as possible
explanation: Sit far enough forward so your arms are slightly bent when you hold the handgrips, which allows pressing on the handlebars without stretching.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.14, 'Body Position'

question: Starting with your right wrist flat while holding the handgrips helps you:
choice_b: Avoid accidentally using too much throttle
explanation: Starting with the right wrist flat helps keep from accidentally applying too much throttle.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.14, 'Body Position'

question: Keeping your knees against the gas tank while riding helps you:
choice_c: Keep your balance as the motorcycle turns
explanation: Keeping your knees against the tank helps maintain balance as the motorcycle turns.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.14, 'Body Position'

question: A typical motorcycle gear pattern is described as:
explanation: A typical gear pattern is 1-N-2-3-4-5, where neutral (N) is selected by a half lift from 1st or a half press from 2nd gear.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.14, 'Shifting Gears'

question: The three-step process for upshifting is:
choice_a: Roll off throttle and squeeze clutch, lift the shift lever, ease out clutch and adjust throttle
choice_b: Squeeze clutch, roll on throttle, release clutch
choice_c: Press shift lever down, release clutch, roll on throttle
choice_d: Roll on throttle, lift shift lever, squeeze clutch
explanation: Upshifting: 1) roll off the throttle while squeezing the clutch, 2) lift the shift lever firmly, 3) smoothly ease out the clutch and adjust the throttle.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.14-15, 'Shifting Gears'

question: Using a lower gear to slow the motorcycle through engine compression is called:
explanation: Shifting to a lower gear causes an effect similar to using the brakes, known as engine braking.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.15, 'Shifting Gears'

question: While stopped, the manual recommends remaining in which gear so you can move out quickly if needed?
explanation: Remain in first gear while stopped so that you can move out quickly if you need to.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.15, 'Shifting Gears'

question: According to the manual, the front brake can provide about what percentage of a motorcycle's total stopping power?
explanation: The front brake is more powerful and can provide at least 70% of total stopping power.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.15, 'Braking'

question: As a motorcycle's weight transfers forward during braking:
choice_a: More traction becomes available at the front wheel, so the front brake can be applied harder
choice_c: The rear brake should be applied harder
explanation: As weight transfers forward, more traction becomes available at the front wheel, so the front brake can be applied harder after braking begins.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.15-16, 'Braking'

question: Maximum straight-line braking is accomplished by:
choice_b: Fully applying both front and rear brakes without locking either wheel
explanation: Maximum straight-line braking is accomplished by fully applying both front and rear brakes without locking either wheel.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.15, 'Braking'

question: An Anti-Lock Braking System (ABS) is designed to:
choice_b: Replace the need for a front brake
choice_c: Prevent wheel lock-up and avoid skids during straight-line panic stops
explanation: ABS prevents wheel lock-up and avoids skids when stopping in straight-line, panic situations by releasing and reapplying hydraulic pressure.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.16, 'Anti-Lock Braking Systems (ABS)'

question: An ABS system can release and reapply brake pressure how many times per second?
explanation: The ABS system is capable of releasing and reapplying pressure more than 15 times per second.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.16, 'Anti-Lock Braking Systems (ABS)'

question: In an integrated braking system:
choice_a: Partial front braking is applied whenever the rear brake is activated
choice_b: The front and rear brakes are entirely independent
choice_c: Only the front brake ever functions
choice_d: The rider must manually balance both brakes at all times
explanation: An integrated braking system is a variation of linked braking in which partial front braking is applied whenever the rear brake is activated.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.16, 'Linked and Integrated Braking Systems'

question: When braking in a curve, as you slow down and reduce lean angle, you should:
choice_a: Apply the same brake pressure as when upright
choice_b: More firmly apply the brakes as more traction becomes available
choice_d: Release the brakes entirely until fully upright
explanation: As you slow and reduce lean angle, more traction becomes available for braking, so you can apply the brakes more firmly.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.15, 'Braking in a Corner'

question: The four steps for better control while turning, in order, are:
explanation: The four steps are SLOW (reduce speed before the turn), LOOK (through the turn), PRESS (on the handgrip to lean), and ROLL (on the throttle to stabilize).
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.16, 'Turning'

question: To turn left using the PRESS step, a rider should:
explanation: Press left handgrip - lean left - go left. Press right handgrip - lean right - go right.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.16-17, 'Turning'

question: In slow, tight turns, riders should:
choice_a: Counterbalance by leaning the motorcycle only while keeping the body straight
choice_b: Lean the body and motorcycle together at the same angle
choice_c: Lean only the body while keeping the motorcycle upright
explanation: In slow, tight turns, counterbalance by leaning the motorcycle only and keeping your body straight, unlike normal turns where rider and motorcycle lean together.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.17, 'Turning'

question: During normal turns at higher speed, the lean angle of the motorcycle:
choice_a: Stays the same regardless of speed
explanation: The higher the speed in a turn, the greater the lean angle required.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.16, 'Turning'

question: Riders should look through a turn by:
choice_a: Turning their shoulders and head together
choice_b: Looking down at the front wheel
choice_c: Turning just their head, keeping eyes level with the horizon
choice_d: Closing their eyes briefly to focus
explanation: Look through the turn to where you want to go, turning just your head, not your shoulders, keeping your eyes level with the horizon.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.16, 'Turning'

question: If you downshift when riding too fast for the lower gear, the likely result is:
choice_d: The motorcycle will lurch and the rear wheel may skid
explanation: If riding too fast when shifting into a lower gear, the motorcycle will lurch and the rear wheel may skid; brakes may be needed to slow enough first.
source_note: TDLR Motorcycle Operator Training Manual 2020-2021, p.14, 'Shifting Gears'
